title: Borrowed Roots
summary: Foundries kept rebuilds legal enough to work by moving one surviving machine's record through many frames; the Authority calls that continuity counterfeit.
body: A root began as a collar number, a set of test marks and a place in the Compact ledger. During the Foundry Winter, damaged machines outlasted all three. Shops shifted serviceable limbs, reactors and cockpits into whatever frame could still walk, then copied the least-disputed number across the result.

The exchange was not a command channel. It was an agreement between yards: one relay carried the borrowed record, one quarry cut a matching plate and one clerk wrote the repair as continuity rather than construction. A single root could keep a district's haulers, pumps and guard machines inside old insurance and ration law.

The Recall Authority reads each copy as a false claim against sealed property. The foundries read it as the paper bridge that kept their settlements alive. By the time a custody tender reaches the original collar, the machine named by it may have become six machines, and six families may depend on which one the warrant decides is real.
